content: At least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in the war in Ukraine by the end of September, and the true death toll is probably closer to 700,000, according to an analysis of leaked data from Russia's own state statistics agency published on Monday. The figures, reported jointly by the independent Russian outlets Mediazona and Meduza, are the most detailed estimate yet of the human cost of the war — and they come from records Moscow itself collected, then stopped publishing. The data was taken in a hack of Rosstat, Russia's Federal State Statistics Service, by the Belarusian hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian group Silent Crow. The two groups announced the breach on November 1, saying they had penetrated not only the agency's website but its internal networks and taken terabytes of files, including mortality records Rosstat had not made public since the middle of 2025. On November 8 they handed journalists a database of 29.7 million records covering nearly all death registrations in Russia's civil registry system from the start of 2021 through August 2026. A second batch followed on November 15: 15 million newer records from Russia's interagency electronic system, covering registrations through September 29. After removing duplicates, amendments and errors, the journalists were left with 11,658,178 unique death records. Of those, about 425,000 carried military causes of death, and roughly 45,000 more people had been declared dead by court decisions, a route often used when a body is missing or has not been recovered. The researchers stress that the 490,000 figure counts only deaths already registered. Because military deaths are often recorded with long delays — sometimes a year or more — they estimate the real number of Russian dead by the end of September stood at around 700,000. By the end of 2025, they put the toll at about 530,000 once unregistered deaths are included, against roughly 350,000 based on registered deaths alone. The journalists say they are confident the data is genuine. They checked it against their own named list of Russian military dead — compiled by Mediazona, the BBC's Russian Service and volunteers from obituaries, social media posts, photographs of graves and official notices — and found matching leaked records for 95.1 percent of the named soldiers whose deaths fell on or before September 29. They also cross-checked the figures against the national probate registry, other leaked civil registry databases, publicly available court rulings and Rosstat's own previously published statistics, and found that their earlier estimates, built from the probate registry, had been largely accurate, even conservative when it came to soldiers missing in action. The remaining gaps were attributed to missing records from Rostov and from occupied parts of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions, errors in the named list, matching failures and delayed registrations. The scale of the toll dwarfs every previous public estimate. In July, the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies put the number of Russian dead at 400,000 to 450,000, with 125,000 to 150,000 on the Ukrainian side. Mediazona's own named list, built case by case since May 2022, stood at 285,881 in early November — a floor, not a total, because it counts only deaths that can be individually confirmed. Ukraine's General Staff, by contrast, claims 1,639,641 Russian troops lost since February 24, 2022, a figure that counts killed and wounded together and that Kyiv updates daily. Rosstat confirmed in early November that its servers had come under attack, but denied that any data had been leaked. The agency has not commented on the new analysis. The figures land at a moment when the war's human cost has become central to the diplomacy around it. The leaked records show a toll that has risen steadily through 2025 and into 2026, with the gap between registered and actual deaths widening as the war drags on — a pattern the researchers attribute to the growing backlog of deaths registered a year or more after they happened. For the Kremlin, which has treated casualty figures as a state secret since the first weeks of the full-scale invasion, the leak removes one of its last shields: the numbers now come from its own bureaucracy. The political question is what a toll of this size does to Russia's ability to keep fighting. Moscow has sustained its war effort through a mix of contract recruitment, high signing bonuses and, since 2022, partial mobilisation, but each new cohort of soldiers is drawn from a population that is increasingly aware of the risks, and the leak gives families and local communities a number to set against official silence. The findings also reframe the negotiations now under way. American envoys have been pressing both sides toward a settlement, and the scale of Russian losses is likely to shape how much pressure Washington believes Moscow can absorb — and how much Kyiv's backers believe the war is costing Russia. What the data cannot answer is the other half of the ledger. There is no comparable leak for Ukrainian losses, and Kyiv, like Moscow, does not publish its own casualty figures. The war's total dead, on both sides, therefore remains unknowable — but for the first time, the Russian half of it is no longer a matter of guesswork. It is written in the state's own registers, and it is far larger than the Kremlin has ever admitted. The photograph accompanying this article shows the Kremlin wall in Moscow, photographed in 2026. summary: Leaked data from Russia's statistics agency Rosstat, analysed by Mediazona and Meduza, shows at least 490,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine by the end of September — with the true toll, once unregistered deaths are counted, likely near 700,000.
title: Leaked Rosstat data puts Russian war dead near 700,000, Mediazona and Meduza report
